hero.title: Experience Virtual Labs at a *Different Dimension*.
hero.description: Explore, interact, and experiment with complex engineering concepts through immersive virtual experiences built for the modern learner.

threeCards.heading: Explore the building blocks of every circuit
threeCards.body: From breadboard to LED to resistor — hands-on 3D interaction with the fundamentals of electronics.

breadboard.body: The solderless breadboard is the starting point for every ECE prototype — snap in components, route jumper wires, and iterate without soldering.

resistor.body: Resistors limit current and set voltage levels. Read the four colour bands — orange, orange, brown, gold — to identify the value and tolerance.

led.body: A light-emitting diode converts current directly into light. Polarity matters: the longer anode lead goes to positive, the flat-side cathode to ground.

featureCards.heading: Store, control and interact — *the next layer of ECE*

capacitor.body: Capacitors store and release charge. The stripe marks the negative lead — always check polarity on electrolytics.
capacitor.label: Energy storage

potentiometer.body: A variable resistor with a dial. Rotate the knob to sweep the wiper between the two end terminals.
potentiometer.label: Controls

pushButton.body: A momentary tactile switch. Current only flows while the cap is pressed — four corner pins straddle the centre gap.
pushButton.label: Input

testimonials.eyebrow: What educators and students are saying.

0.text: Before VLabs, students would spend half the lab session just getting the hardware to behave. Now they walk in having already verified the circuit virtually, and we can focus entirely on what the experiment is actually teaching.

1.text: Building a full-wave bridge rectifier on a physical breadboard takes 40 minutes and someone always burns an LED. On VLabs I had the circuit running, sweep measured, and ripple factor calculated in under ten minutes.

2.text: The 8085 emulator is exactly what was missing. Students can single-step through assembly, watch registers change, and actually understand the fetch-decode-execute cycle instead of just memorising it for the exam.
